title: A weekly circle
tomorrow: what do you even say when you visit someone who's sick?

segments.voice: Yesterday, two days: Monday and Thursday, a small effort held firmly and gently. Today's effort isn't one you make alone.

A group chat goes silent for weeks, then lights up the second someone types: same time next week? Some things only happen when people keep showing up. Amira quit her Wednesday study circle in the fall. Too busy, she said, and she can read on her own. So does a circle really matter, or is studying alone just as good?
screen: `SAME TIME NEXT WEEK?` → `SHE QUIT IN THE FALL.` → `ALONE, OR GATHERED?`

segments.voice: The tradition answers in a report in Sahih Muslim. No group gathers in one of the houses of God, reciting the Book and studying it together, but four things happen: tranquility, sakina, comes down on them; mercy covers them; angels surround them; and God mentions them among those with Him. Notice it isn't only about learning. It's about what settles on the room. And why weekly? In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Mas'ud gave his reminders every Thursday. People asked him to make it every day. He said no: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ spaced out his teaching so they wouldn't grow bored. A circle that meets once a week, on purpose, so people keep coming back. Now a neighbor. Jordan's grandmother goes to a Wednesday night Bible study, and there's a line Christians quote for exactly this, from Matthew's Gospel, in the King James words: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." What's shared: the sense that something is present when people gather that isn't there when you sit alone. What's honestly different: in Matthew, Jesus speaks of himself in their midst, and Christians hear Christ present; in the hadith, it's tranquility, mercy, angels and God's remembrance, and Muslims don't speak of the Prophet being there. Two traditions, each in its own words, both pulling up a chair. That's every week.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you'd study with, or one circle you've drifted from. Send them a short message now: a question about something you read, or simply, same time next week? If there's no one yet, write down one place a circle might be waiting: a mosque, a library, a friend's kitchen table.

segments.voice: A weekly circle, a halaqa: people who meet on a set day to read and study together, and on whom, the report says, tranquility comes down.
Keep it near: every week, the circle is where the settling happens. One day left in the week's turn.

howItsDone: Muslims gather in weekly study circles (halaqas) at mosques, campuses and homes, reading a passage of the Qur'an or hadith together and talking it through, often with a teacher.

chat.meaning: In Muslim's report, tranquility, mercy and angels come to people studying together; Ibn Mas'ud kept his circle weekly so people wouldn't tire.

sakina.meaning: tranquility: a calm that comes down

Ibn Mas'ud.meaning: a companion of the Prophet who taught the Qur'an

Matthew.meaning: one of the four Gospels in the Christian Bible
